related_questions.question: Why do I keep getting headaches after COVID?
related_questions.snippet: Sometimes, headaches keep happening even after you've gotten over COVID. Long COVID is a chronic condition that lasts weeks, months, or even years after a COVID illness. People with long COVID have symptoms that linger, and long COVID headache is one of them. This can happen even if you had a mild case of COVID.

related_questions.question: When should I be worried about headaches?

text_blocks.snippet: You should be concerned about headaches when they are sudden and severe, or accompanied by other concerning symptoms like fever, stiff neck, confusion, or vision changes. Headaches that worsen over time, interrupt daily life, or follow a head injury also warrant medical attention.
snippet_highlighted_words: when they are sudden and severe, or accompanied by other concerning symptoms like fever, stiff neck, confusion, or vision changes

text_blocks.snippet: When to seek immediate medical attention (emergency care):

list.title: Sudden and severe headaches:
list.snippet: Especially those reaching maximum intensity within seconds or minutes, could indicate a brain bleed or stroke, according to Supreme Vascular and Interventional Clinic.

list.title: Headaches accompanied by fever, stiff neck, confusion, seizures, double vision, weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking:
list.snippet: These could be signs of a serious infection, meningitis, or other neurological problems, according to Houston Methodist and the Mayo Clinic.

list.title: Headaches that start right after a head injury:
list.snippet: This could indicate a concussion or other traumatic brain injury.

list.title: Headaches that wake you up from sleep:
list.snippet: Especially if severe or early in the morning, they could be a sign of a serious underlying condition.

list.title: Headaches that get progressively worse:
list.snippet: Even if not initially severe, persistent or worsening headaches should be evaluated, says the Mayo Clinic.

text_blocks.snippet: When to see a doctor for headaches (non-emergency):

list.title: Headaches that interfere with your daily life:
list.snippet: If headaches are frequent, intense, or prevent you from working, attending school, or engaging in social activities, according to Keck Medicine of USC you should seek medical advice.

list.title: New headaches after age 50:
list.snippet: Headaches appearing for the first time later in life may warrant investigation, says Supreme Vascular and Interventional Clinic.

list.title: Headaches accompanied by other symptoms:
list.snippet: Such as vision changes, tingling sensations, skin rash, dizziness, or neck pain, notes KidsHealth.

list.title: Headaches that don't respond to over-the-counter pain relievers:
list.snippet: If your usual headache remedies are not effective, consult with your doctor.

related_questions.question: Why do I have a headache every day?

text_blocks.snippet: Frequent, daily headaches can stem from various factors, including lifestyle choices, stress, and underlying health conditions. Identifying the specific cause is crucial for effective management.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle choices, stress, and underlying health conditions

list.title: Stress:
list.snippet: Stress is a major trigger for tension headaches, causing muscle tension in the neck and shoulders, which the brain interprets as head pain.

list.title: Sleep Issues:
list.snippet: Inadequate or disrupted sleep, or even oversleeping, can trigger headaches, including migraines and tension headaches.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: Skipping meals, dehydration, and certain foods like aged cheese, processed meats, and alcohol can contribute to headaches.

list.title: Medication Overuse:
list.snippet: Frequent use of headache medication can lead to rebound headaches.

list.title: Sensory Triggers:
list.snippet: Bright lights, loud noises, and strong smells can trigger migraines or worsen existing headaches.

list.title: Underlying Conditions:
list.snippet: Conditions like sinusitis, TMJ disorders, and even more serious issues like brain tumors or infections can cause headaches.
Headaches that are severe, sudden, or accompanied by fever, stiff neck, or neurological symptoms.
Headaches that disrupt daily life or don't respond to over-the-counter pain relievers.
Changes in the pattern of your headaches.
Headaches that occur after a head injury.
Identify and manage stress: Practice relaxation techniques, exercise, or seek professional help if needed.
Establish a regular sleep schedule: Aim for 7-9 hours of quality sleep per night.
Maintain a healthy diet and stay hydrated: Avoid skipping meals and drink plenty of water.
Avoid known headache triggers: Keep a headache diary to track potential triggers and adjust your lifestyle accordingly.
Consider over-the-counter pain relievers: Use them as directed and consult with a doctor if they are not effective.
Consider medical advice: If your headaches are frequent, severe, or accompanied by other symptoms, seek professional medical advice.
